chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his narrators whom he mentioned, saying:

Gold for gold and silver for silver, by weight in equal measure, with no preference of one over the other. Silver can be exchanged for gold and gold for silver as you wish, hand to hand, and there is no harm in that. Credit (nasi'ah) is not permissible [for same-kind exchange]. Gold and silver can be sold for other than them by weight or measure or count or otherwise, hand to hand and on credit, all of which are permissible.

And whatever is measured or weighed whose origin is one, there is no preference of one over the other in measure or weight. If the origin of what is measured differs, there is no harm in exchanging two for one hand to hand, but credit is disliked. [And if the origin of what is weighed differs, there is no harm in exchanging two for one hand to hand, but credit is disliked.]

And whatever is measured by what is weighed, there is no harm in it, hand to hand and on credit, all is permissible. And whatever is counted by number and not measured or weighed, there is no harm in it, two for one hand to hand, and credit is disliked.
And he said: If its origin is one, and even if the origin of what is counted differs, there is no harm in it, two for one hand to hand and on credit, all is permissible.
And whatever is counted or not counted, there is no harm in it with what is measured or weighed, hand to hand and on credit, all is permissible.
And whatever has one origin and is measured or weighed, if something comes out of it that is neither measured nor weighed, there is no harm in it hand to hand, but credit is disliked.

This is because cotton and flax, their origin is weighed, and their yarn is weighed, but their garments are not weighed. So cotton has no preference over yarn, and since their origin is one, it is not valid except like for like and weight for weight. When garments are made from it, it becomes valid hand to hand.
And for garments, there is no harm in exchanging two shirts for one shirt, even if their origin is one, hand to hand, but credit is disliked.
And if it is cotton and flax, there is no harm in it, two for one hand to hand, and credit is disliked.
And if the garments are of cotton and flax, there is no harm in it, two for one hand to hand and on credit, both are permissible.
And there is no harm in exchanging cotton and flax garments for wool, hand to hand and on credit.
And whatever is from animals, there is no harm in it, two for one, even if its origin is one, hand to hand, and credit is disliked.
And if the origin of the animals differs, there is no harm in it, two for one hand to hand, and credit is disliked.
And if an animal is exchanged for goods, and you take delivery of the animal and delay the goods, there is no harm in it. And if you take delivery of the goods and delay the animal, it is disliked.
And if you sell an animal for an animal or with an addition of a dirham or goods, there is no harm, and there is no harm in taking delivery of the animal and delaying the dirhams.
And a house for two houses, and a jarib of land for two jaribs, there is no harm in it hand to hand, but credit is disliked.

He said: And in what is measured and weighed, one does not look except to the general custom, and is not taken by the specific [custom]. If a people measure meat and measure nuts, it is not considered with them, because the origin of meat is to be weighed and the origin of nuts is to be counted.
ai.seo_question: What are the rules for exchanging gold, silver, and other goods in Shia Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elaborates on the principles of riba al-fadl and riba al-nasi'ah, establishing that same-kind commodities require exact equality and immediate possession, while different-kind exchanges permit flexibility in quantity and timing. It highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the 'origin' (asl) of a commodity to determine its measurement method, ensuring that transactions avoid the hidden interest traps prevalent in pre-Islamic trade practices. The text serves as a foundational legal guide for distinguishing between permissible barter and prohibited usury in commercial dealings.
